paras: The Queenstown lynching threats were threats in August 1881 to lynch Black suspects in the killing of two children, Joseph and Lizzie Fisher, at Queenstown in the county outside Washington, D.C. Early dispatches said men at a Washington market talked of lynching a missing Black farm hand, while the local investigation turned to an elderly Black woman, Christina Taylor, whom police later hurried to jail ahead of would-be lynchers. No lynching is reported, and the murder itself was called one of the most shocking crimes in the area in years.

The children, aged six and three, lived with their uncle Joseph Fisher, a market man whose farm lay on the Bunker Hill road near Brooks' Station. On Saturday, August 6, the adults went to market and left the children alone at the farm, as they often did. Christina Taylor, her daughter Rose and her grandson Thomas Goff lived as Fisher's tenants in a stone house at the farm gate.

Fisher came home about six that evening and found both children dead near the house with their skulls crushed, an axe lying nearby. A Washington dispatch in the New Haven Morning Journal and Courier said a Black hand in Fisher's employ was missing and that search parties scoured the county with the help of the police. The same dispatch described "the wildest commotion" that night at the K Street market, where butchers and hucksters said they wanted to leave "to take part in lynching the scoundrel if he were caught." Shorter versions in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer and the Bismarck Tribune repeated that parties were searching for the missing employee.

The Washington papers made no mention of a missing hand. Instead, police arrested Christina and Rose Taylor that night and Thomas Goff the next day, after farm hands said they had seen the older woman leaving the Fisher house. The coroner's jury, which sat on August 7 and 10, could not say "positively" who killed the children but found that suspicion pointed "strongly" to Christiana Taylor. On August 11 she told Captain Vernon and Archibald White that "the devil" had put it in her head to kill the children and that she had used a piece of wood, not the axe or the washboard. According to the Montgomery County Sentinel, quoting the Washington Post, Lieutenant Johnson then drove her to jail in a grocer's wagon to put her beyond the reach of "certain parties" waiting to lynch her.

Taylor was committed to jail, Thomas Goff was released, and Rose Taylor was held as a witness for the grand jury due to meet on September 12. Rose testified to her mother's "giddy spells," and some, "particularly the colored people," claimed the old woman was insane, a view also gaining ground among the police. Black residents gathered nightly near the police station; they doubted Taylor's guilt but wanted the killer brought to justice.
A Richmond paper later reported that she alternately confessed and denied the killing; no report of an indictment or trial appears.

The first telegraphic reports centered on an unnamed Black suspect, and the Bismarck Tribune's telegram stated flatly that the murder was "perpetrated last evening by a negro." Only the New Haven version carried the market men's lynching talk, printed without comment.

Washington's Evening Star, Evening Critic and National Republican printed inquest testimony at length, and the Star called Taylor "a crabbed old crone." The Critic also quoted a Black officer, Mounted Policeman West, who doubted the evidence against the women. After the confession the Star called the killing "simply the act of a fiend" and urged "the extreme penalty provided by law."
The confession ran as "A Horrible Confession" in the New-York Tribune and "A Murder Confessed" in the Daily Gazette, and the Sentinel reprinted it a week later.

The first wire dispatches blamed a missing Black farm hand, while the Washington papers and a Portland dispatch reported the arrest of two Black women. The local reports, resting on arrests and sworn inquest testimony, are the stronger evidence. Early reports blamed the axe, detectives proposed the washboard, and Taylor said she used a stick that was never found.

bases: The only anti-Black violence reported is lynching talk: market men said they would lynch a missing Black farm hand if caught (A1), and police moved Christina Taylor to jail ahead of parties waiting to lynch her (A19); no one was attacked.
No one was killed or seized; the reports describe threats to lynch a suspect in the children's murder (A1, A19), so the standard definition is not met.

The murder, arrests, inquest and confession are corroborated across many papers (A4, A6, A12, A14, A15), but each lynching threat rests on one report: the market talk on a single wire dispatch (A1) and the threat against Taylor on the Sentinel's Post account (A19).

framing.detail: The first dispatch reported the market men's lynching talk without comment and expected 'the guilty party' to be arrested soon.
The Bismarck Tribune's telegram stated as fact that a negro employee 'perpetrated' the murder.
Washington dailies printed inquest testimony at length but called Taylor 'a crabbed old crone' and her grandson 'a stupid-looking black boy'.
The Evening Star editorial called the killing 'the act of a fiend' and urged the extreme legal penalty, not lynching.
The confession ran as 'A Horrible Confession' and 'A Murder Confessed' in New York and elsewhere.
